en.headline: From OA to Security — A Trajectory Built on One Conviction
paragraphs: My career started inside Korea Aerospace Industries' closed network, tracking patch schedules for the closed-network Linux fleet on an Excel sheet. Repeating the same work every week led to one conviction: the value of security engineering is not hoping incidents never happen, but lowering risk through repeatable procedures, automation, and evidence. I then consecutively earned RHCSA, LPIC-1, and Linux Master Level 2 to rebuild my Linux foundation, and carried that base into hands-on automation work.

At Metanet M Platform I picked up Ansible and Python, organizing the NAC policy deployment procedure for contact-center operations. At Jointree, I applied NSX-T microsegmentation to Kookmin University's next-generation information system, reducing east-west traffic blind spots and reorganizing the NAC and DLP detection policies. The tools changed, but the principle didn't: any task that repeatedly takes manual effort is a candidate for runbooks.

At Quantec Investment Management's Financial Security Data Center (FSDC), responding to Financial Supervisory Service audits taught me that security infrastructure is not about setting things up once, but about being able to present current state and change evidence with data during audits and incidents. Tuning DB access-control queries and validating a PB platform POC were both about explaining system state with data and leaving a trail behind every change.

Most recently, in the Nextrade exchange security track, I was engaged continuously from build (Gaonnuri) through automation (ITCEN CTS). I built network segmentation and endpoint security controls, supported Korean Financial Services Commission main-license review response, standardized security appliance configuration with Ansible Role, and connected Splunk ES detection rules, alert workflow notifications, FortiManager API policy lookups, and Claude AI-assisted review to design the recognition, classification, and alerting flow for security events.

Next, I am widening the scope of automation tooling from security appliances and scripts toward MCP and Edge runtimes. My homelab — Cloudflare Workers, MCP, Grafana, 1Password — runs on Terraform-managed IaC where I experiment with patterns in which an MCP tool makes the first pass over repetitive security-response items. In my next chapter, I want the security problem to come before the tool, and to take on the role of turning that problem into a repeatable engineering structure.
en.closing: I will carry this trajectory — built on a single question about the limits of repetitive work — into the next problem your security infrastructure needs to solve, and answer it the same way.
